items.title: Hubert Laws — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: George Coleman was playing there... That was a group for me.

ctx.x: When we get into ’73, starting off the year in January with Ron Carter, Blues Farm, yet another one of those that looms large, because he’s got Richard Tee on organ. He’s all over the map. Ron Carter, another one of those who’s bridged both worlds. When did you meet Ron? It seems like you have a sympatico as well.

Yeah. I call Ron every now and then, because Ron is so subtle, but he’s so supportive. He’s subtle but supportive of every group. He’s not the greatest soloist, improvising soloist, but he’s such as support[ive] – he plays the right notes at the right spot, and his sound is – I like the way he connects his notes. The notes are connected. They overlap, in a sense. I met Ron first – I remember telling Ron, “I love all your work with Miles Davis.” That’s when I really knew about him.
